title: Majestic Combination
reviewNotes: Montages, captions and complete native diagrams reviewed. Begin after Ka3 at123 seconds in the complete nine-piece later diagram: White Kc2/Rb7/Nd4 against Ka3/Qe7/d7/d6/e6/h7. Native28 establishes this full board; Ra7+ forces Kb4, and native30/31 confirm the resulting diagram, native32 shows Nc6+, and native33 the illustrated Kc5 reply. The rook attacks the queen through d7, so the pawn is relatively pinned to the queen, not legally pinned to its king: dxc6 is legal and must be checked. The selected fork and independent capture continuations retain all four black pawns until an actual capture. A complete finite White strategy enumerates every Black reply through exact supported wins. Earlier Bd6/cxd6, the earlier king-and-rook route and the other queen-capture branch remain outside this selected conversion proof.
transcript: Fools will resign. Wise players might make a draw, but only a true genius would be able to win from this position. You see, black does have a queen, but any decent player would be able to hold a draw with a bishop, knight, and rook for the queen. It is going to be tricky to hold back all of these pawns, but not impossible. But what is surprising is the fact that white is actually completely winning [music] this position thanks to an incredible resource that starts with the brilliant bishop to D6. [music] A quite beautiful move that sacrifices the bishop two different ways. Now, of course, if the queen takes the bishop, this would make no sense after knight to B5 check, forking the king and queen, and picking up the queen like this, winning the game for white. But naturally, black can pick up the bishop like this, and now there is going to be no fork. So, what was the purpose of this sacrifice? Black still has an entire queen, and now the situation seems to be worse [music] because we're also down an entire bishop. But you see, in chess, a piece is only powerful if you can use it in any way. And in this case, after this diagonal is closed, this queen has no way to come and help the black king. But that said, checkmating this king is not easy feat. We can play king [music] to C3 and threaten a checkmate in one move like this. Now, of course, if the king comes to A4, this is not going to help in any way. This is still a checkmate. The knight is defending this square. But of course, the king can go down to A2. Now, trying to chase him would result into nothing. The king can simply come back up, and this is going to be a draw by repetition. But white starts playing a quite mysterious sequence of moves. Rook B2 check, forcing the king back up because, of course, if the king comes down, this is a checkmate. But after the king comes to A3, now white plays rook to B7, a mysterious move. This is threatening the checkmate one more time. But we have already seen that the king can go down and avoid the checkmate. White plays king to C2, and the king comes back up. Is this going to be a draw by repetition? Well, not exactly because white plays rook to A7. What? This is not a checkmate. The king escapes. But actually, the rook is pinning the D pawn, allowing knight to C6 with [music] yet another fork. White is going to pick up the queen and win the game. [music] If you love incredible chess, follow for more.
